3. Study 1: Large-Scale Monte Carlo Simulation (97,200 Datasets)

>Study 1: Large-Scale Monte Carlo Simulation (97,200 Datasets)

3.1 Study 1 Method: Experimental Design and Data Generation

To rigorously evaluate the algorithmic accuracy of rEGA against a known population reference structure (Ground Truth), we designed a large-scale Monte Carlo simulation study using R (v. 4.5.0; R Core Team, 2025) and a full nested factorial design across 972 experimental conditions (comprising 108 unidimensional cells with 𝐾 = 1 where 𝜙 is analytically fixed at .00, and 864 multidimensional cells with 𝐾 ∈ {2,4} and 𝜙 ∈ {. 00, .30, .50, .70}). Each condition was replicated 100 times, generating a total of 97,200 analyzed datasets (the complete parameter grid and reproducible code are detailed in Supplementary Material S3). Both the data-generating process and the analytical pipeline were executed in R 4.5.0 using the deterministic parallel pseudorandom number generator L 'Ecuyer-CMRG = 11 (L'Ecuyer, 1999; Morris et al., 2019), achieving a 100.0% convergence rate with zero lost runs. The number of replications per condition (𝑅 = 100) was established following methodological standards in network psychometrics (Epskamp & Fried, 2018; Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023), ensuring a Monte Carlo Standard Error (MCSE) below ±0.94% when estimating marginal dimensional accuracy and below ±0.058% when evaluating reliability bias.

The experimental conditions systematically manipulated seven key psychometric factors, with magnitudes selected to reflect the empirical variability observed in test development and validation (Comrey & Lee, 2013; Garrido et al., 2013; Golino et al., 2020b):

First, the number of underlying latent dimensions was set to 𝐾 ∈ {1,2,4} factors, spanning from strict unidimensionality to complex multidimensionality (Golino & Epskamp, 2017; Golino et al., 2020a). Including unidimensional structures (𝐾 = 1) is critical because traditional community detection algorithms applied to networks frequently incur artificial overfragmentation when evaluating single-factor scales (Christensen et al., 2023b; Golino et al., 2020a).

Second, the number of items per dimension was manipulated across 𝑝 𝑐 ∈ {4,8} items, configuring instruments with a total variable count of 𝑝 ∈ {4,8,16,32}, which expanded dynamically up to 𝑝 = 35 items under the addition of perturbation nodes in regimes P1 and P2. This spans from brief screening subscales (𝑝 𝑐 = 4) to extended measurement dimensions (𝑝 𝑐 = 8), following standardized factorial design specifications in psychometric network simulations (Christensen et al., 2024; Golino et al., 2020b; Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023).

Third, sample size was varied across three representative levels: 𝑁 ∈ {250,500,1000} participants, allowing us to examine the performance of support-constrained maximum likelihood refitting (𝐊 ̂refit ) in both moderate or clinical samples (𝑁 = 250) and large samples (𝑁 ≥ 500), in keeping with methodological recommendations for partial correlation networks (Golino & Epskamp, 2017; Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023). Fourth, population factor loading magnitudes were set at 𝜆 ∈ {. 40, .55, .70}, uniformly representing a discrimination range spanning from networks with weak or fair signal (𝜆 = .40) to highly cohesive structures (𝜆 = .70), in accordance with the standard taxonomy of Comrey and Lee (2013) and Garrido et al. (2013).

Fifth, three topological scenarios of structural contamination and conditional residual variance were manipulated to evaluate graph robustness under violations of simple structure: (a) P0 (Clean), corresponding to a pure reference structure without perturbation terms (Golino & Epskamp, 2017); (b) P1 (Bridge Noise), which introduces bridging variance and peripheral noisy items to test the model's capacity to attenuate complex inter-community edges without inducing over-factoring (Christensen & Golino, 2021; Christensen et al., 2023b); and (c) P2 (Local Dependence), which incorporates local dependence doublets driven by lexical redundancy between items, modeled via residual correlations of 𝜃 𝑖𝑗 ∈ {. 20, .40}, to verify whether refitting the precision diagonal prevents the formation of spurious micro-dimensions (Christensen et al., 2023; Golino et al., 2020a).

Sixth, inter-factor correlation intensity was varied across 𝜙 ∈ {. 00, .30, .50, .70} to evaluate algorithmic sensitivity to overlap among substantive dimensions (Christensen et al., 2023b; Golino & Epskamp, 2017), noting that for the unidimensional condition (𝐾 = 1) this correlation was analytically fixed at 𝜙 = .00 given the absence of competing latent dimensions. Finally, all conditions were evaluated under both a continuous Gaussian response format and a 5point polytomous Likert format, ensuring ecological validity for ordinal data commonly encountered in applied assessment (Garrido et al., 2013; Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023).

3.2 Analytic Plan and Methodological Evaluation Criteria

Each of the 97,200 simulated datasets was processed using four comparative dimensionality estimation and community detection algorithms: (1) rEGA-Leiden (Traag et al., 2019), executed on the Topological Purity-Weighted Adjacency Matrix 𝐀 rEGA ; (2) conventional EGA based on the Walktrap algorithm (Golino & Epskamp, 2017; Pons & Latapy, 2006); (3) conventional EGA based on the Louvain algorithm (Blondel et al., 2008; Golino et al., 2020a); and (4) Parallel Analysis with Principal Components (PA-PCA; Garrido et al., 2013; Horn, 1965), using the 95th percentile rule across 100 random permutation matrices. Walktrap and Louvain were included given their status as conventional standards within the EGA framework (Christensen et al., 2023b; Golino et al., 2020b), whereas PA-PCA serves as the classical benchmark in dimensionality assessment.

To quantitatively evaluate the performance of the methods against the population reference structure (Ground Truth), five standard quantitative metrics from the psychometric simulation literature were computed.

First, dimensionality recovery accuracy was evaluated via the Percentage of Correct Classification (PC%; Garrido et al., 2013; Golino & Epskamp, 2017), defined as the proportion of replications in which the estimated number of dimensions coincided exactly with the population value (𝐾 ̂= 𝐾), where 100.0% reflects perfect accuracy. Second, the magnitude and direction of error in estimating the number of factors were quantified via the Mean Absolute ; Golino et al., 2020a Golino et al., , 2020b;; Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023), where values near 0.000 indicate no deviation from the true structure.

Third, the accuracy of item assignment to their respective communities was measured using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI; Hubert & Arabie, 1985; Rand, 1971), which evaluates concordance between the estimated community partition and the true population partition while correcting for chance agreement. The ARI ranges from . 000 (random agreement) to 1.000 (identical recovery of the community structure). ; Epskamp et al., 2018b; Wysocki & Rhemtulla, 2019), which measures accuracy in deducing Markov nodal error relative to the systematic attenuation of penalized estimators (Pötscher & Leeb, 2009).

Fifth, the accuracy of metric reliability estimated by rEGA was quantified via Total Coefficient Gamma Bias (Bias Γ = Γ ̂𝑡 -Γ 𝑡,population ; Henry, 2026; McNeish, 2018), compared directly against the bias of Coefficient Alpha (Cronbach, 1951) and Coefficient Omega (McDonald, 1999), where deviations from . 000 indicate whether the proposed coefficient incurs overestimation due to local dependence or underestimation due to uncontrolled random error (Sánchez-Meca et al., 2021) Finally, to evaluate the relative importance of the manipulated factors on quantitative performance metrics without falling prey to 𝑝-value triviality from the large replication count (97,200 datasets), Factorial Analyses of Variance (ANOVAs) were conducted on each aforementioned metric. Following simulation standards in network psychometrics (Golino et al., 2020b; Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023; Jiménez et al., 2023), the magnitude of each experimental factor and its interactions was quantified via partial eta-squared (𝜂 𝑝 2 ), identifying substantial effects as those exceeding Cohen's (1988) threshold (𝜂 𝑝2 ≥ .14) for a large effect size.

4. Study 2: Multi-Sample and Multi-Instrument Empirical Validation

>Study 2: Multi-Sample and Multi-Instrument Empirical Validation

4.1 Study 2 Method: Samples, Participants, and Instruments

To evaluate the empirical applicability, cross-sample validity, and diagnostic capacity of rEGA in real-world data, we conducted a secondary analysis across three independent, screened samples totaling 𝑁 = 3,200 Colombian adult participants.

The databases were drawn exclusively from the open-science repository of Ruiz et al. (2024), collected via non-probabilistic sampling under ethical protocols approved by the institutional review board of the Fundación Universitaria Konrad Lorenz (Bogotá, Colombia), with prior informed consent obtained across three distinct cohorts: Sample 1 (Community; 𝑁 = 2,398 in AAQ-II / 2,393 in DASS-21; 62.4% women; age 𝑀 = 28.6 years, 𝑆𝐷 = 9.4, range = 18--68; 63.8% undergraduate/college graduates, 18.4% postgraduate, and 17.8% secondary education); Sample 2 (Clinical; 𝑁 = 358; 68.2% women; age 𝑀 = 34.1 years, 𝑆𝐷 = 11.2, range = 18--65); and Sample 3 (General; 𝑁 = 444 in AAQ-II only; 66.7% women; age 𝑀 = 27.6 years, 𝑆𝐷 = 9.6, range = 18--62; 61.3% secondary/technical education, 25.9% undergraduate, and 12.8% postgraduate).

Two widely used self-report psychometric instruments were evaluated: First, the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II (AAQ-II; Bond et al., 2011) was administered using the Spanish adaptation validated for Latin America by Ruiz et al. (2016). The AAQ-II comprises 7 items (operationally labeled PI1 to PI7). Items are rated on a 7-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (never true) to 7 (always true), where higher scores reflect greater psychological inflexibility. Although the AAQ-II was designed as a unidimensional measure of Psychological Inflexibility, it has been the subject of ongoing debate regarding its items' putative lack of discriminant validity against affective distress (Ruiz et al., 2024; Wolgast, 2014) and its pronounced vulnerability to artificial over-fragmentation induced by lexical local dependence between redundant item pairs (e.g., items 1-4 and 2-3; Ruiz et al., 2016). This property makes the AAQ-II an ideal case study for evaluating across all samples rEGA's capacity to diagnose lexical doublets and preserve the global unidimensionality of the test (Phase 2A).

Second, the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scales-21 (DASS-21; Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995) was evaluated using the Spanish version validated for Hispanic populations by Daza et al. (2002). The DASS-21 is a 21-item tripartite scale organized into three latent dimensions of 7 items each: Depression (D1 to D7; e.g., anhedonia and lack of meaning), Anxiety (A1 to A7; e.g., physiological hyperarousal and subjective anxious experience), and Stress (S1 to S7; e.g., tension and irritability). Items are rated on a 4-point Likert scale assessing symptom frequency over the past week, from 0 (did not apply to me at all) to 3 (applied to me very much, or most of the time). The structure of the DASS-21 is notable in psychometric network research (Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023) for featuring transdiagnostic bridge symptoms alongside peripheral somatic indicators (e.g., A1 "dryness of mouth"). This multidimensional configuration is optimal for evaluating, across Samples 1 and 2, the detection of defective items and the decomposition of inter-community bridging variance (Phase 2B).

4.2 Empirical Statistical Analysis Plan

Processing and analysis of the empirical data in Study 2 were conducted in R (v. 4.5.0; R Core Team, 2025) using the psychometric network package rEGA (v. 1.0.0; Huerta-Huacchahuilca, 2026), configured under a standardized analytical sequence across all three samples for the AAQ-II and across Samples 1 and 2 for the DASS-21: (a) Network estimation and dimensional structure: We computed the baseline polychoric correlation matrix (cor_auto), active support selection via EBICglasso (𝛾 = .50; Foygel & Drton, 2010), debiased refitting via Restricted Maximum Likelihood (𝐊 ̂refit ), derivation of the topological purity-weighted adjacency matrix (𝐀 rEGA ), and community identification via the Leiden algorithm, evaluating dimensional partition quality with the Total Entropy Fit Index (TEFI; Golino et al., 2020a) and quantifying concordance between the recovered structure and canonical theoretical dimensions via the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI; Hubert & Arabie, 1985) Using the parallelized resampling routine boot.rEGA, we executed 𝐵 = 500 independent nonparametric case-resampling bootstrap replications (Efron, 1979; Epskamp et al., 2018a) with the L'Ecuyer-CMRG generator under a fixed deterministic seed (seed = 11; L'Ecuyer, 1999; Morris et al., 2019) to determine item replication stability (IS), 95% confidence intervals, and dimensional consistency, preserving the joint empirical distribution and ensuring robustness to polytomous data skewness without imposing multivariate normality assumptions (Burger et al., 2023; Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023); and (e) Cross-sample nodal profile invariance: We quantified nodal profile replicability between the community (𝑁 = 2,393) and clinical (𝑁 = 358) populations on the DASS-21 via Pearson correlations (𝑟) across the vectors of Markov uniqueness (𝜓 𝑖 2 ) and within-factor communality (ℎ 𝑖 2 ), given the instrument's sufficient degrees of freedom (𝑝 = 21, 𝑑𝑓 = 19; Epskamp et al., 2018a; Forbes et al., 2017; Jamison et al., 2024); whereas on the AAQ-II (𝑝 = 7), cross-sample invariance was verified through the ordinal consistency of the error hierarchy (𝜓 𝑖 2 ) and item replication stability (IS) across the three evaluated samples (𝑁 = 3,200).

5. Results

>Results

5.1 Study 1: Algorithmic Recovery, Markov Precision, and Analysis of Variance

The overall results of the 97,200-dataset Monte Carlo simulation are synthesized in Tables 1, 2, 3, and 4, and illustrated in Figures 1, 2, 3, and 4.

5.1.1 Dimensionality Recovery Accuracy and Topological Resilience

Across all 972 evaluated experimental conditions (Table 1; Figure 1), rEGA-Leiden demonstrated superior accuracy in recovering the population dimensional structure, achieving an overall Percentage of Correct Classification of 87.65% (𝑀 = .877, 𝑀𝑑𝑛 = 1.000, 𝑆𝐷 = .229) and a Mean Absolute Error of MAE = .128 (𝑀𝑑𝑛 = .000). By contrast, conventional EGA based on Walktrap obtained an overall accuracy rate of 64.81% (MAE = .512), EGA with Louvain reached 69.77% (MAE = .421), and traditional Parallel Analysis (PA-PCA) achieved 71.32% (MAE = .389). Moreover, whereas Walktrap and Louvain exhibited a systematic tendency toward over-factoring (MBE = +.793 and MBE = +.681, respectively), rEGA-Leiden reduced classification bias to near-zero levels (MBE = +.075, 𝑀𝑑𝑛 = .000) while attaining a higher Adjusted Rand Index (ARI = .800, 𝑀𝑑𝑛 = .950).

Under the regime of contamination by bridging variance and noisy items (P1 Bridge Noise; Table 1), methods relying on unweighted adjacency matrices showed pronounced vulnerability. In unidimensional structures (𝐾 = 1) with weak factor loadings (𝜆 = .400), EGA-Walktrap and EGA-Louvain collapsed to accuracy rates of 15.00% to 21.80% and 6.70% to 8.90%, respectively. Conversely, the topological purity-weighted adjacency matrix (𝐀 rEGA ) protected the graph structure, enabling rEGA-Leiden to sustain accuracy rates between 81.70% and 89.00% within this regime. In the presence of local dependence driven by lexical doublets (P2 Local Dependence), rEGA-Leiden maintained accuracy rates between 70.80% and 91.90% across all levels of local dependence, whereas Walktrap and Louvain dropped to ranges of 17.30% to 32.50%. Finally, comparisons across response formats confirmed the metric equivalence of rEGA-Leiden in continuous Gaussian data (84.90% accuracy in P0) and ordinal polytomous data (87.10% in P0).

5.1.2 Tripartite Nodal Diagnosis and Recovery of Markov Uniquenesses

The capacity of rEGA to classify the topological function of each node and recover the unbiased precision matrix is reported in Table 2 and Figures 2 and 4. In identifying the tripartite diagnostic space (Figure 2), the model showed high discriminative accuracy. Under moderate sample sizes (𝑁 ≥ 500) and typical loadings (𝜆 ≥ .550), rEGA's sensitivity in isolating pure noise nodes (𝜓 𝑖 2 → 1.000) reached 99.38% overall (𝑀𝑑𝑛 = 1.000, 𝑆𝐷 = .017).

Simultaneously, sensitivity for detecting genuine inter-community bridging variance (𝛽 𝑖 2 > .200) stood at 91.92% overall (𝑀𝑑𝑛 = .990), while specificity in retaining pure core nodes within their source dimensions (ℎ 𝑖2 ≫ 𝛽 𝑖 2 ) reached 86.76% overall (𝑀𝑑𝑛 = .958, retaining between 91.40% and 100% when 𝜆 ≥ .550).

In reconstructing the parameters of the underlying stochastic process (Table 2; Figure 4), the Restricted Maximum Likelihood refitting stage (𝐊 ̂refit ) yielded a Root Mean Square Error of RMSE 𝜓 = .037 (𝑀𝑑𝑛 = .034) in the clean reference condition (P0, with the overall average across noise conditions standing at RMSE 𝜓 = .035; Table 2), representing a 54.80% reduction in estimation error relative to classical factor uniqueness (𝜃 𝑖 , RMSE = .082). As sample size increased from 𝑁 = 250 to 𝑁 = 1,000, RMSE 𝜓 decreased monotonically from . 045 to . 018 (. 054 to . 021 in the global aggregate), confirming convergence of order 𝒪(1/√𝑁). Similarly, the relative rank-ordering of nodal indicators estimated via Spearman's rank correlation yielded a mean value of 𝑟 𝑠 = .795 (𝑀𝑑𝑛 = .843), reaching . 933 in samples of 𝑁 = 1,000.

5.1.3 Unbiasedness of Gamma Coefficients and Graph Standard Error

In the evaluation of metric reliability (Table 3; Figure 3), Total Coefficient Gamma (Γ 𝑡 ) and Within-Community Coefficient Gamma (Γ 𝑐 ) exhibited near-zero mean bias (Bias Γ = -.007, 𝑀𝑑𝑛 = -.004, 𝑆𝐷 = .010), proving three times more stable than McDonald's Coefficient Omega (𝑆𝐷 = .030, Bias ranging from -.061 to +.129) and Cronbach's Coefficient Alpha (𝑆𝐷 = .025). Overall, the Root Mean Square Error of Coefficient Gamma (RMSE Γ = .0299) was lower than that of Coefficient Omega (RMSE 𝜔 = .0343).

Under the regime of local dependence from correlated residuals (P2 Local Dependence; Figure 3), the presence of lexical doublets induced artificial overestimation in Coefficient Alpha (Bias 𝛼 = +.071 to +.103) and Coefficient Omega (Bias 𝜔 = +.051 to +.078). Conversely, by computing Γ 𝑐 from the refitted matrix 𝐊 ̂refit and the resolvent operator, rEGA isolated the excess local covariance along the uniqueness diagonal (𝜓 𝑖 2 ), preserving the unbiasedness of the estimator (Bias Γ = -.010 to -.002). Finally, the estimated Standard Error of Measurement of the Graph (SEM 𝑡 raw ) recorded a mean value of 2.095 points on the observed raw scale, closely matching the true population parameter (true_sem = 1.980 points; and 1.994 vs. 1.986 in continuous data; Table 3).

5.1.4 Decomposition of Experimental Effects via Factorial ANOVA

The Factorial Analyses of Variance (ANOVAs) conducted on the performance criteria (Table 4) revealed that the choice of estimation algorithm (Method: rEGA vs. Walktrap vs. Louvain vs. PA-PCA) was the primary source of variation in dimensional classification accuracy (PC%), accounting for 41.2% of the total variance (𝜂 𝑝2 = .412, 𝑝 < .001). The topological contamination regime represented the second primary source of influence (𝜂 𝑝2 = .284, 𝑝 < .001), followed by factor loading magnitude (𝜆; 𝜂 𝑝2 = .195, 𝑝 < .001) and sample size (𝜂 𝑝2 = .128, 𝑝 < .001). Regarding metric reliability accuracy (Bias Γ ), the topological contamination regime and loading intensity exerted the dominant main effects (𝜂 𝑝2 = .314 and 𝜂 𝑝2 = .142, respectively), confirming that rEGA mitigates measurement error distortion.

5.2 Study 2 Results: Multi-Sample Empirical Validation

5.2.1 Phase 2A: Unidimensionality, Lexical Redundancy, and Reliability in the AAQ-II

The numerical results from the analysis of the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II (AAQ-II) across Samples 1, 2, and 3 are presented in Tables 5, 7, and 9, and illustrated in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

Estimating the network structure via the topological purity-weighted adjacency matrix (𝐀 rEGA ) identified a unidimensional solution in Community Sample 1 (𝑁 = 2,398; Figure 5, Panel A) and General Sample 3 (𝑁 = 444; Figure 5, Panel C). In Community Sample 1 (𝑁 = 2,398), all methods (rEGA-Leiden, Walktrap, and Louvain) properly recovered theoretical unidimensionality (𝐾 = 1,ARI = 1.000; Table 8). However, in General Sample 3 (𝑁 = 444), Walktrap and Louvain over-fragmented the scale into two dimensions (ARI = .612), whereas the weighted matrix 𝐀 rEGA directly sustained the unidimensional solution (𝐾 = 1,ARI = 1.000). In turn, in Clinical Sample 2 (𝑁 = 358; Figure 5, Panel B), heightened local dependencies initially split the graph into three micro-clusters grouped around item pairs PI1-PI4, PI2-PI3, and the PI5-PI7 block (ARI = .412), whereupon rEGA ruled out over-factoring through the Nodal Triad leakage diagnostic.

The decomposition under the Law of Conservation of the Nodal Triad (Figure 6) detailed the proportional variance distribution across the scale's seven items. In Sample 1, mean withinfactor communality was ℎ2 = .688 (signal variance) and mean Markov conditional uniqueness was 𝜓2 = .312 (Table 7). In Sample 3, equivalent mean proportions were observed (ℎ2 = .644; 𝜓2 = .356). Conversely, in Clinical Sample 2, the three-dimensional partition registered an elevation in inter-community bridging variance (𝛽2 = .346)-unlike the other samples, which recorded null values (𝛽2 = .000)-exceeding mean within-factor communality (ℎ2 = .267). Consequently, dimensional reliability coefficients remained low (Γ 𝑐 = .631 for Dimension 1, Γ 𝑐 = .371 for Dimension 2, and Γ 𝑐 = .601 for Dimension 3; Table 5).

Evaluating the global parameters and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI, in brackets) via boot.rEGA (𝐵 = 500 replications; Figure 7; Table 9) showed that, when assessing the global unidimensional structure, the Global Graph Noise Ratio was Ψ 𝒢 = .312 in Sample 1, Ψ 𝒢 = .387 in Sample 2, and Ψ 𝒢 = .356 in Sample 3. The Total Network Coefficient Gamma reached values of Γ 𝑡 = .940 [. 935, .944] in Sample 1; Γ 𝑡 = .916 [. 900, .931] in Sample 2; and Γ 𝑡 = .928 [. 916, .940] in Sample 3. Finally, the raw-score Standard Error of Measurement of the Graph was estimated at SEM 𝑡 raw = 2.537, SEM 𝑡 raw = 2.906, and SEM 𝑡 raw = 2.602 points in Samples 1, 2, and 3, respectively (Table 5).

5.2.2 Phase 2B: Multidimensionality, Nodal Diagnosis, and Invariance in the DASS-21

The empirical analysis results for the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scales-21 (DASS-21) across Samples 1 and 2 are detailed in Tables 5, 6, 8, and 9, and illustrated in Figures 8, 9, and 10. First, network structure estimation via the topological purity-weighted adjacency matrix (𝐀 rEGA ) is presented in Figure 8 (Panels A and B) and Table 8. The rEGA-Leiden algorithm exactly recovered the theoretical three-dimensional tripartite structure (Anxiety, Depression, and Stress) in Community Sample 1 (𝑁 = 2,393; ARI = 1.000,TEFI = -3.634), achieving high global graph reliability (Γ 𝑡 = .970 [95% CI: . 968, .972]) and dimensional reliability values ranging from Γ 𝑐 = .575 (Stress, 7 items) to Γ 𝑐 = .758 (Depression, 7 items; Table 5). By contrast, the Walktrap algorithm over-segmented the network in the community sample, generating a spurious dimension (ARI = .619). In Clinical Sample 2 (𝑁 = 358), rEGA estimated four interconnected dimensions (TEFI = -5.551).

Second, the 100%-stacked Law of Conservation of the Nodal Triad decomposition across all 21 items is shown in Figure 9 (Panels A and B) and Table 6. rEGA isolated that item A1 ("dryness of mouth") exhibited high Markov conditional uniqueness in both samples (𝜓 A12 = .667 in Sample 1; 𝜓 A12 = .755 in Sample 2), represented by the dominance of the noise segment in its nodal bar. This elevated conditional uniqueness preceded its low stability under bootstrap resampling (IS = .378 in Sample 2). Conversely, items D2 ("initiative"), S3 ("nervous energy"), and S6 ("intolerance") registered high proportions of inter-community bridging variance (𝛽 D22 = .452, 𝛽 S32 = .411, 𝛽 S62 = .497 in Sample 1) accompanied by moderate levels of conditional uniqueness (𝜓 𝑖2 ≤ .502).

Third, bootstrap inference and the cross-sample nodal profile invariance analysis between the Community Sample (𝑁 = 2,393) and the Clinical Sample (𝑁 = 358) are presented in Figure 10 and Table 9. Correlating the nodal profile across both independent samples revealed high linear cross-sample replicability: 𝑟 = .936 (𝑝 < .001) for Markov conditional uniqueness (𝜓 𝑖 2 ), 𝑟 = .961 (𝑝 < .001) for within-factor communality (ℎ 𝑖 2 ), and 𝑟 = .727 (𝑝 < .001) for intercommunity bridging variance (𝛽 𝑖

6. Discussion

The present study introduced, algebraically formalized, and validated Reliability Exploratory Graph Analysis (rEGA), an analytical framework designed to integrate conditional measurement error decomposition and metric reliability estimation within Exploratory Graph Analysis. Although network psychometrics has established a conceptually sound alternative to common-cause models through Gaussian Markov Random Fields (GGM; Borsboom et al., 2021; Epskamp et al., 2017 Epskamp et al., , 2018b;; Schmittmann et al., 2011) and the EGA paradigm has shown notable effectiveness in dimensionality identification (Christensen et al., 2023b; Golino & Epskamp, 2017; Golino et al., 2020a Golino et al., , 2020b)), existing workflows operated on the partial correlation matrix while discarding the conditional precision diagonal. This omission precluded analytically isolating each item's residual variance and quantifying the metric precision of scores without invoking latent variable assumptions (Christensen et al., 2020; Epskamp et al., 2017 Epskamp et al., , 2018a)). The Reliability Exploratory Graph Analysis (rEGA) model formalizes nodal variance decomposition through the Neumann-Markov resolvent operator (𝐐 = (𝐈 -𝛀) -1 ) and the Law of Conservation of the Nodal Triad (ℎ 𝑖 2 + 𝛽 𝑖 2 + 𝜓 𝑖 2 ≡ 1.000). This decomposition distinguishes within-community signal, inter-community bridging, and Markov conditional uniqueness, enabling the derivation of native reliability estimators (Γ 𝑐 , Γ 𝑡 , Ψ 𝒢 ) alongside standardized (SEM 𝑐 std ) and raw-score (SEM 𝑡 raw ) standard errors of measurement. Thus, rEGA quantifies the precision of composite scores directly from the perspective of Gaussian networks (Lauritzen, 1996; Whittaker, 1990).

6.1 Parametric Recovery Mechanisms and Resilience to Topological Violations

The ANOVA decomposition in Study 1 demonstrated that the choice of analytical method is the primary determinant of dimensional accuracy (𝜂 𝑝2 = .412), conditional uniqueness recovery (𝜂 𝑝2 = .486), and reliability unbiasedness (𝜂 𝑝2 = .528), substantially outweighing the effects of sample size and factor loading magnitude. This advantage stems from analytically correcting two core vulnerabilities documented in network estimation. On the one hand, although regularization via EBICglasso is optimal for selecting the active edge support (ℰ 𝜆 ), the 𝐿 1 penalty systematically shrinks retained parameters and distorts the precision diagonal (Epskamp & Fried, 2018; Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023; Pötscher & Leeb, 2009; Wysocki & Rhemtulla, 2019). In this respect, rEGA returns to the original spirit of Foygel and Drton (2010) by decoupling topological selection from parameter estimation; empirical evidence confirms that extracting Markov uniqueness directly from EBICglasso overestimates conditional error (RMSE 𝜓 = .158 marginal), whereas support-constrained restricted maximum likelihood refitting (𝐊 ̂refit ; Dempster, 1972; Drton & Perlman, 2004) restores asymptotic consistency of order 𝒪(1/√𝑁), reducing by 54.8% the error incurred by traditional approaches that conflate common-cause factor uniqueness (𝜃 𝑖 = 1 -𝜆 𝑖 2 ) with true Markov conditional uniqueness (𝜓 𝑖2 = 𝑄 𝑖𝑖 -1 ; RMSE 𝜓 = .037 vs. . 082).

On the other hand, incorporating the Topological Purity-Weighted Adjacency Matrix (𝐴 𝑖𝑗 rEGA ) accounts for the resilience of rEGA-Leiden against the over-fragmentation tendency of conventional community detection algorithms (MBE = +.793 in Walktrap and +.681 in Louvain vs. +.075 in rEGA). As noted by Golino et al. (2020a Golino et al. ( , 2020b) ) and Christensen et al. (2023a Christensen et al. ( , 2023b)), in unidimensional structures with weak loadings (𝜆 = .40), bridge noise (P1), or local dependence doublets (P2), unweighted partial correlation matrices assign equal topological credibility to all links, allowing residual covariances to trap random walks and reducing the accuracy rates of Walktrap and Louvain below 32.5%. By evaluating the resolvent operator 𝐐 = (𝐈 -𝛀) -1 beforehand, rEGA identifies items with weak systemic integration (𝜓 𝑖 2 → 1.0) and selectively attenuates their edges via the factor √(1 -𝜓 𝑖 2 )(1 -𝜓 𝑗 2 ), isolating pure noise nodes with 99.4% sensitivity and sustaining correct classification rates between 70.8% and 91.9% across both continuous and polytomous data. Given that simply swapping community detection algorithms on unweighted matrices yields only marginal variations in accuracy (1% to 3% between Leiden and Walktrap; Christensen et al., 2024), the 20% to 36% advantage achieved by rEGA confirms that Markov error shrinkage integrated into 𝐴 𝑖𝑗 rEGA -rather than the mere choice of community optimizer-is the primary driver of topological resilience.

In turn, the findings from Study 1 clarify the role of the Gamma Coefficients (Γ 𝑐 , Γ 𝑡 ) and the Standard Error of Measurement of the Graph (SEM 𝑡 raw ): these metrics do not serve as dimensionality retention indices, but rather as quantifiers of the metric precision of composite scores once the graph architecture has been established. Under local dependence from lexical doublets (P2), classical common-cause coefficients such as 𝛼 and 𝜔 suffer systematic overestimation (Bias = +.051 to +.103) because a single-factor model absorbs the residual covariance of the redundant pair as if it were true construct variance (Christensen et al., 2023a; McNeish, 2018). Conversely, because they are derived from 𝐊 ̂refit and the resolvent operator, Γ 𝑐 and Γ 𝑡 isolate excess conditional covariance along the uniqueness diagonal (𝜓 𝑖 2 ), preserving an unbiased estimate of the error-free variance proportion (Bias Γ = -.010 to -.002) and accurately reproducing the population standard error of measurement in raw-scale units (SEM 𝑡 raw = 2.095 vs. 1.980).

6.2 Resolution of Empirical Artifacts, Nodal Dominance, and Metric Score Precision

Study 2 extends these mechanisms to real-world data analysis, showing how rEGA links internal structure diagnosis with measurement error quantification on observed scores. In applied practice, conventional community detection algorithms (such as Walktrap, Louvain, or Leiden) optimize modularity functions (𝑄) that by definition assign a null value (𝑄 = 0) to an undivided graph (𝐾 = 1; Blondel et al., 2008; Pons & Latapy, 2006; Traag et al., 2019), such that any localized increase in conditional density induced by lexical overlap tends to force a spurious topological subdivision (𝑄 > 0). This dynamic was evident in the evaluations of the AAQ-II: whereas in Samples 1 and 3 the purity-weighted matrix (𝐴 𝑖𝑗 rEGA ) directly contained fragmentation and recovered the theoretical unidimensionality posited by Bond et al. (2011), in Clinical Sample 2 (𝑁 = 358) the intensification of local partial correlations initially divided the graph into three micro-clusters organized around the lexically redundant pairs PI1-PI4 and PI2-PI3 (Ruiz et al., 2016 (Ruiz et al., , 2024;; Wolgast, 2014) In this regard, rEGA establishes a foundational epistemological distinction: the structural validity of a graph partition is not adjudicated by the magnitude of reliability coefficientswhose function is not to declare the existence of dimensions but to quantify random score error-but rather by the Nodal Triad Dominance Rule or Structural Leakage Criterion (𝛽 2 vs. ℎ 2 ). Auditing the decomposition ℎ 𝑖 2 + 𝛽 𝑖 2 + 𝜓 𝑖 2 ≡ 1.000 on the clinical partition of the AAQ-II revealed that mean inter-community bridging variance (𝛽2 = .346) systematically exceeded within-community communality (ℎ2 = .267). This leakage ratio (𝛽 2 /ℎ 2 > 1.000) algebraically demonstrates that more than half of the systematic variance in each putative micro-cluster dissipates toward the rest of the graph rather than reverberating internally, depriving the subgroups of structural autonomy. Once the sub-partition was ruled out for lacking internal validity, metric evaluation of the unidimensional composite score via the global resolvent operator revealed high and consistent structural reliability across all three samples (Γ 𝑡 = .940, .916, and . 928), bounding individual score uncertainty through raw-score standard errors of measurement of SEM 𝑡 raw = 2.537,2.906, and 2.602 points, respectively.

Complementarily, evaluating a multidimensional instrument such as the DASS-21 (Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995) demonstrated both item-level diagnostic precision and the proper interpretation of Γ 𝑐 and Γ 𝑡 across coupled subscales. At the topological level, rEGA exactly recovered the theoretical tripartite structure in the community population (ARI = 1.000,TEFI = -3.634 vs. ARI = .619 in Walktrap) and resolved the ambiguity noted in the literature regarding how to distinguish defective items from bridge symptoms (Burger et al., 2023; Christensen & Golino, 2021; Epskamp et al., 2018a). The Nodal Triad proved that the low bootstrap stability of somatic item A1 ("dryness of mouth", IS = .378) stemmed from dominant Markov conditional uniqueness (𝜓 A12 = .667 to . 755), whereas the assignment fluctuations of D2 ("initiative"), S3 ("nervous energy"), and S6 ("intolerance") reflected genuine transdiagnostic bridging variance (𝛽 𝑖2 = .411 to . 497) combined with low conditional error (𝜓 𝑖2 ≤ .502). In Clinical Sample 2 (𝑁 = 358), the intensification of this transdiagnostic coupling led the topological optimizer to delineate four communities by splitting the Stress block (TEFI = -5.551). Despite differences in clinical severity between the two populations, the nodal architecture exhibited strong linear cross-sample invariance (𝑟 = .936 for 𝜓 𝑖 2 and 𝑟 = .961 for ℎ 𝑖 2 ), qualifying critiques regarding the putative non-replicability of psychopathology networks (Forbes et al., 2017) when the graph is estimated free of 𝐿 1 bias via 𝐊 ̂refit.

Likewise, the analysis of DASS-21 scores clarifies the psychometric interpretation of reliability coefficients in multidimensional networks and challenges the mechanical application of static cutoffs inherited from Classical Test Theory, such as the universal requirement of values exceeding . 70 (critiqued by Lance et al., 2006; McNeish, 2018). Because the Within-Community Coefficient Gamma (Γ 𝑐 ) is computed on the isolated local resolvent operator 𝐐 𝑐 = (𝐈 𝑐 -𝛀 ̂𝑐𝑐 ) -1 , it analytically removes all inter-community transmission pathways (𝛽 𝑖 2 ).

Consequently, Γ 𝑐 is not equivalent to a subscale's unconditioned 𝛼 or 𝜔 coefficient (.88 to .94, which absorb cross-reverberation covariance with other syndromes), nor does it incur the denominator penalty of the bifactor subscale hierarchical omega coefficient (𝜔 ℎ𝑠 , which treats general-factor comorbidity as error in the denominator and collapses toward zero as 𝛽 𝑖 2 → 1 -𝜓 𝑖 2 ; see Theorem 4 in Supplementary Material S1; Jiménez et al., 2023; Reise et al., 2012).

Instead, Γ 𝑐 constitutes the network analogue of the subscale omega coefficient (𝜔 𝑠 ; McDonald, 1999) topologically purified over the conditioned subgraph 𝐐 𝑐 . From this metric perspective, the fact that Depression records Γ 𝑐 = .758 to . 789 (SEM 𝑐 raw = 2.62 to 2.69 points) while Anxiety (Γ 𝑐 = .621 to . 653, SEM 𝑐 raw = 2.91 to 3.08 points) and Stress (Γ 𝑐 = .575 to . 601, SEM 𝑐 raw = 3.12 to 3.24 points) show moderate values does not call into question the structural existence of the three dimensions. Rather, it precisely indicates that while the Depression score possesses high isolated specific precision, a substantial fraction of the reliable variance in Anxiety and Stress scores stems from their transdiagnostic co-activation (𝛽 𝑖 2 ) with the rest of the system, which is fully captured when evaluating the precision of the global composite score via Γ 𝑡 (. 960 to . 970, SEM 𝑡 raw = 2.46 to 3.81 points).

6.3 Network Epistemology, REGEMA Guidelines, and Preservation of Canonical Scales

From an epistemological and normative standpoint, computing Γ 𝑐 , Γ 𝑡 , and the SEM simultaneously in multidimensional instruments does not presuppose the existence of a secondorder general latent variable (𝑔). In a Markov Random Field, covariance across symptom domains emerges from activation diffusion circulating through bridge nodes (𝛽 𝑖 2 ), governed algebraically by the higher-order powers of the partial correlation matrix in the Neumann series (𝐐 = ∑ 𝛀 𝑚 ∞ 𝑚=0 ).

Accordingly, Γ 𝑡 quantifies the proportion of total systematic variance relative to stochastic noise (Ψ 𝒢 ) in the composite index of symptom severity across the complete network. Having these metric estimators resolves indirect reliability induction in the network literature at its root: faced with the theoretical incompatibility of applying 𝛼 or 𝜔 to conditional graphs (Christensen et al., 2020; McNeish, 2018), applied studies routinely reported bootEGA structural consistency (a configurational frequency of cluster replication) as an improper metric substitute. By providing empirically computed precision coefficients (Γ 𝑐 , Γ 𝑡 ) and standard errors of measurement (SEM 𝑐 raw , SEM 𝑡 raw ), rEGA enables the construction of individual confidence intervals, Spearman-Brown disattenuation corrections (AERA, APA, & NCME, 2014, Standards 1.21 and 11.8; Henry, 2026; Spearman, 1904a), and the future formal integration of network psychometrics into Reliability Generalization meta-analyses under the REGEMA guidelines (Sánchez-Meca et al., 2021; Vacha-Haase, 1998).

Additionally, this framework provides a methodological safeguard against the measurement flexibility warned against by Elson et al. (2023), characterized by the proliferation of ad hoc scale versions that fragment cumulative science. In conventional bootEGA applications, researchers frequently drop items with low replication stability (IS) or reassign items across subscales based on the particular partition of their sample (Jamison et al., 2024). However, as established in Standards 2.0 and 2.2 of the AERA, APA, and NCME (2014), reliability is a property of scores within a specific population rather than an immutable constant of the test. Truncating or restructuring a standardized scale because an item oscillates between communities in a given sample conflates sampling variability or clinical population dynamics with an instrument defect, undermining content validity and cross-study comparability (Forbes et al., 2017; Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023).

Through the Law of Conservation of the Nodal Triad, rEGA demonstrates that low assignment stability in hard-partitioning algorithms stems from two opposite phenomena requiring differentiated analytical treatment. On the one hand, in transdiagnostic bridge nodescharacterized by high Global Topological Purity (ℎ 𝒢,𝑖2 = ℎ 𝑖 2 + 𝛽 𝑖 2 ) driven predominantly by bridging variance (𝛽 𝑖 2 ), as seen in items D2, S3, and S6 of the DASS-21-oscillation between adjacent clusters in clinical samples reflects genuine comorbidity across syndromes (Borsboom et al., 2021). In strict adherence to AERA, APA, and NCME (2014) guidelines and the caveats of Elson et al. (2023), such indicators should neither be removed nor reassigned to construct ad hoc subscales, but rather preserved within their canonical theoretical dimensions, insofar as rEGA explicitly accounts for their bridging flow within Γ 𝑐 , Γ 𝑡 , and the SEM.

On the other hand, when a node is dominated by substantial Markov conditional uniqueness (𝜓 𝑖 2 > ℎ 𝒢,𝑖 2 , such as item A1 of the DASS-21), its instability reflects conditional stochastic error alone. Whereas topological reduction procedures such as Unique Variable Analysis (UVA; Christensen et al., 2023a) suggest combining locally dependent variables into reduced composite scores, merging a noisy item with other nodes in the presence of high Markov uniqueness is counterproductive because it injects and propagates error variance (𝜓 𝑖 2 ) into the combined indicator. Instead, rEGA automatically quantifies and attenuates such excess noise in the matrix 𝐴 𝑖𝑗 rEGA and in the computation of SEM 𝑡 raw , preserving the integrity of the canonical scale without resorting to manual pruning or arbitrary cutoffs.

6.4 Practical Guidelines for Applied Researchers

In keeping with editorial recommendations for methodological transfer in quantitative psychology (Burger et al., 2023; Golino et al., 2020b; Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023), we synthesize the application of the R package rEGA (version 1.0.0; Huerta-Huacchahuilca, 2026; see reproducible code in Section S2 of the Supplementary Material) into a four-stage decision protocol.

In the first stage, corresponding to graph estimation and sample support, the researcher fits the model using the function rEGA(data, algorithm = "leiden", gamma = 0.50, seed = 11) on polychoric or Pearson correlation matrices (cor_auto). Because the accuracy of restricted maximum likelihood refitting (𝐊 ̂refit ) and the recovery of Markov conditional uniqueness (𝜓 𝑖 2 ) follow an error reduction rate of order 𝒪(1/√𝑁), maximizing sample size is recommended in high-dimensional networks or clinical samples with elevated comorbidity to narrow the variability of the resolvent operator and ensure community detection stability.

In the second stage, focused on structural evaluation via the Nodal Dominance Rule, the compositional decomposition ℎ 𝑖 2 + 𝛽 𝑖 2 + 𝜓 𝑖 2 ≡ 1.000 should be inspected before accepting the graph partition. If the algorithm delineates multiple communities but the Nodal Triad reveals systematic variance leakage (𝛽 ̅ 2 > ℎ ̅ 2 ), the leakage ratio (𝛽 ̅ 2 /ℎ ̅ 2 > 1.000) proves that the subdivision is an artifact induced by modularity optimization in the presence of lexical local dependence, indicating that the unidimensional structure or canonical theoretical architecture should be retained.

In the third stage, addressing the functional audit of indicators without resorting to ad hoc test truncation, items are classified according to the relative dominance of their components into: (a) core items, defined by the dominance of within-factor communality over bridging variance (ℎ 𝑖 2 > 𝛽 𝑖 2 ) and low Markov uniqueness, acting as pure dimension markers; (b) transdiagnostic bridge nodes, characterized by bridging variance comparable to or exceeding within-factor communality (𝛽 𝑖2 ≥ ℎ 𝑖 2 ) alongside high global topological purity (ℎ 𝒢,𝑖2 = 1 -𝜓 𝑖 2 ), which should be retained within their canonical theoretical dimensions without removal even if they exhibit bootstrap assignment instability; and (c) noisy or defective items, identified by the dominance of Markov conditional uniqueness (𝜓 𝑖 2 > ℎ 𝒢,𝑖 2 ), whose conditional error is attenuated by the adjacency matrix 𝐴 𝑖𝑗 rEGA and documented for future content revisions of the instrument.

In the fourth stage, concerning the metric reporting of reliability, measurement error, and bootstrap inference, the function boot.rEGA(rEGA.obj = fit, iter = 500, type = "resampling", seed = 11) is executed to derive point estimates and 95% confidence intervals for Γ 𝑐 , Γ 𝑡 , Ψ 𝒢 , and SEM raw , accompanied by the observed standard deviation (𝑆 𝑌 ) of composite scores in the analyzed sample. Rather than applying rigid universal cutoffs from Classical Test Theory, researchers should interpret Within-Community Coefficient Gamma (Γ 𝑐 ) as the isolated specific precision of the syndrome within its conditioned subgraph 𝐐 𝑐 (the topologically purified network analogue of subscale 𝜔 𝑠 , immune to the comorbidity-induced collapse of bifactor 𝜔 ℎ𝑠 ; see Theorem 4 in Supplementary Material S1), Total Coefficient Gamma (Γ 𝑡 ) as the precision of global systemic severity, and use the Standard Error of Measurement of the Graph (SEM 𝑡 raw ) to construct individual confidence intervals and disattenuate relationships with external variables, in strict compliance with the REGEMA guidelines (Sánchez-Meca et al., 2021) and the AERA, APA, and NCME (2014) Standards.

6.5 Limitations, Future Directions, and Conclusion

The scope of the present study is subject to methodological boundaries that outline priority avenues for the research agenda in network psychometrics. First, the current formulation of the resolvent operator is framed within Gaussian Graphical Models (GGMs) for continuous and ordered polytomous data; generalizing the nodal variance framework to discontinuous or non-Gaussian structures, such as Ising binary networks and Mixed Graphical Models (MGMs; Haslbeck & Waldorp, 2020), represents a natural extension of the model. Second, because restricted maximum likelihood refitting (𝐊 ̂refit ) conditions precision recovery on the active support initially selected by EBICglasso, the behavior of debiasing in small-sample scenarios with weak edges motivates exploring the integration of non-convex estimators or Bayesian selection schemes (Wysocki & Rhemtulla, 2019). Third, the interaction between nodal topological purity and community detection algorithms opens opportunities to examine optimization functions tailored to psychometric topology by isolating hybrid combinations to deepen these findings, as well as to link the rEGA reliability framework with complementary local dependence methodologies (Christensen et al., 2023a), structural invariance tests (Jamison et al., 2024), and longitudinal models (Christensen & Golino, 2021). Finally, because rEGA evaluates a closed compositional system sensitive to graph density, we refrained from setting universal static cutoffs; future research may further investigate the dynamic calibration of decision thresholds as a function of network structural characteristics (Burger et al., 2023; Elson et al., 2023). Transparency, Openness, and Reproducibility Statement

This study complies with the APA Journal Article Reporting Standards for Quantitative Research (JARS-Quant; Appelbaum et al., 2018), the reporting standards for cross-sectional psychological network analyses (Burger et al., 2023), the ADEMP framework for Monte Carlo simulation studies (Morris et al., 2019). The primary empirical datasets analyzed in Study 2 are publicly available in the Open Science Framework (OSF) repository deposited by Ruiz et al. (2024) at https://osf.io/2tf9k/. All reproducible R scripts for the Study 1 Monte Carlo simulation (97,200 datasets; deterministic parallel RNG seed L'Ecuyer-CMRG = 11 in R version 4.5.0), Study 2 empirical analyses with SHA-256 data integrity verification, mathematical proofs (Supplementary Material S1), and tabular audit workbooks are openly available in the project OSF repository (https://osf.io/[INSERT_PROJECT_ID]) and in the Supplementary Materials accompanying this article.

Ethics Approval and Informed Consent

All empirical procedures involving human participants across Samples 1, 2, and 3 were conducted in strict accordance with the Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct of the American Psychological Association (APA) and the Declaration of Helsinki. The primary data collection protocol was formally reviewed and approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of the Fundación Universitaria Konrad Lorenz (Bogotá, Colombia; Ruiz et al., 2024), and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to data collection. 72.40% 0.281 48.20% 0.710 52.10% 0.620 58.30% 0.510 𝜆 = .55 91.80% 0.082 72.30% 0.380 78.40% 0.310 79.10% 0.290 𝜆 = .70 99.20% 0.008 94.50% 0.080 96.20% 0.050 95.80% 0.060 Inter-Community Bridge Noise (𝑃 1 ) 𝜆 = .40 64.80% 0.390 12.50% 1.420 18.20% 1.210 42.10% 0.890 𝜆 = .55 88.20% 0.120 45.10% 0.810 51.80% 0.720 68.40% 0.450 𝜆 = .70 98.30% 0.020 64.80% 0.490 71.20% 0.380 84.20% 0.210 Local Item Dependence (𝑃 2 ) 𝜆 = .40 70.80% 0.310 18.20% 1.380 24.50% 1.150 48.20% 0.780 𝜆 = .55 89.50% 0.110 41.20% 0.890 48.90% 0.780 69.50% 0.410 𝜆 = .70 99.50% 0.005 62.40% 0.520 69.80% 0.410 82.10% 0.240 Note. Parenthetical values represent positive reliability inflation bias resulting from unmodeled residual covariances violating common-cause unidimensionality assumptions. In non-clinical samples (Samples 1 and 3), the AAQ-II functions as a pure unidimensional system (𝛽 𝑖2 = .000). In clinical settings (Sample 2), the apparent dimensional fragmentation into 3 micro-communities is driven by local wording overlap artifacts (PI2/PI3 and PI6/PI7 doublets), where inter-community bridging variance (𝛽 ̅2 = .346) dominates over within-community communality (ℎ ̅2 = .267), demonstrating the structural spuriosity of the sub-dimensions. This topological diagnosis supports single-factor scoring, for which Total Network Gamma (Γ 𝑡 = .916 to . 940) quantifies high metric score reliability across all samples. Community detection algorithms: Walktrap (Pons & Latapy, 2006; random walks = 4 on unweighted partial correlation matrix), Louvain (Blondel et al., 2008; modularity optimization on unweighted partial correlation matrix), and rEGA-Leiden (Traag et al., 2019; Leiden algorithm executed on the purity-weighted adjacency matrix 𝐀 rEGA ). * In AAQ-II Sample 2 (Clinical) and Sample 3 (General), unconstrained graph partitioning initially detected micro-clusters driven by wording overlap doublets (PI2/PI3 and PI6/PI7); however, the Nodal Triad diagnostic (intercommunity bridging variance dominating over within-community communality, 𝛽 ̅ 2 > ℎ ̅ 2 ) demonstrated the structural spuriosity of the sub-dimensions, supporting single-factor scoring (𝐾 ̂= 1 * , ARI = 1.000), for which Total Network Gamma (Γ 𝑡 = .916 to . 940) quantifies high metric score reliability across all samples.

Fourth, fidelity in recovering the precision matrix and conditional residual variance was assessed via the Root Mean Square Error of Uniqueness Recovery (RMSE 𝜓 = ; (b) Nodal variance decomposition: We evaluated the 100%-stacked Law of Conservation of the Nodal Triad (ℎ 𝑖 2 + 𝛽 𝑖 2 + 𝜓 𝑖 2 ≡ 1.000), classifying each item's function into within-factor signal variance (ℎ 𝑖 2 ), inter-community bridging variance (𝛽 𝑖 2 ), and Markov conditional uniqueness (𝜓 𝑖 2 ); (c) Estimation of structural reliability and measurement error: We computed the Within-Community Coefficient Gamma (Γ 𝑐 ), Total Network Coefficient Gamma (Γ 𝑡 ), Global Graph Noise Ratio (Ψ 𝒢 ), and the Standard Error of Measurement of the Graph in both standardized (SEM 𝑐 std ) and raw-score metrics (SEM 𝑐 raw and SEM 𝑡 raw ); (d) Bootstrap inference and stability:

Notwithstanding these considerations, rEGA bridges the longstanding divide between conditional graph topology and psychometric measurement precision theory. By recovering the debiased precision diagonal via 𝐊 ̂refit , formulating the Law of Conservation of the Nodal Triad (ℎ 𝑖 2 + 𝛽 𝑖 2 + 𝜓 𝑖 2 ≡ 1.000), and deriving the Gamma Coefficients (Γ 𝑐 , Γ 𝑡 ) alongside the Standard Error of Measurement of the Graph (SEM 𝑡 raw ), this framework provides an exact analytical solution for decoupling internal structure validation from score error estimation. In doing so, rEGA preserves the integrity of canonical psychological scales against ad hoc modifications, securing individual error metrics and ensuring strict compliance with REGEMA guidelines and international measurement standards.
